title: He didn’t fall.
paragraphs:
He didn’t fall.
He didn’t fail.
He stepped down.
And that’s what makes it uncomfortable.
Because most of us only know how to let go when life forces our hands. When doors close. When influence fades. When the crowd disappears.
But John the Baptist?
He walked away while the crowd was still chanting his name.
Let that sit.

This was a man forged in the wilderness—dust on his skin, fire in his bones, truth on his tongue. He didn’t preach what was safe. He preached what was true. And people came in waves. Hungry. Broken. Curious. Convicted.
They crossed deserts just to hear him.
Some believed he was the Messiah.
That’s how powerful his presence was.
And then—
Jesus stepped into the scene.

No announcement.
No campaign.
Just quiet authority wrapped in human flesh.
And suddenly… everything shifted.
The same people who once surrounded John began following Jesus. The same voices that once echoed John’s name started whispering about another.
And here’s where the tension breaks open:
John’s own disciples came to him, concerned.
“Rabbi, the one you testified about… He’s baptizing, and everyone is going to Him” (John 3:26).
Translation?
“You’re losing them.”
And right there—right in that moment—John had a choice.

Protect his platform…
Or surrender to his purpose.

Compete…
Or complete his assignment.

Cling…
Or release.
And John said something that echoes through eternity:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

No bitterness.
No insecurity.
No quiet resentment hidden behind spiritual language.

Just clarity.
Just surrender.
Just joy.
He even said his joy was now complete—not when people followed him—but when they followed Christ (John 3:29).
That is not natural.
That is supernatural.
Because the human heart craves significance. We want to be seen. We want to matter. We want to be the voice people remember, the face people follow, the name people say.
And John had all of that.
Yet he let it go.
Why?
Because he knew something we forget:
He was never the Savior.
He was the signpost.
And signposts don’t compete with the destination.
They point.
Some of you are exhausted right now—not because God has abandoned you, but because you’re holding onto something you were only meant to steward for a season.

A position.
A platform.
A version of yourself that God is already calling you beyond.
And you feel the shift.

You see others rising.
You feel the attention moving.
You sense the quiet whisper of God saying, “It’s time.”
And everything in your flesh resists it.
Because decreasing feels like dying.
But here’s the Gospel truth:
It is.
Jesus said, “Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).
The Kingdom is built on this paradox—death that leads to life, surrender that leads to freedom, decreasing that leads to becoming.
John’s story doesn’t end on a stage.
It ends in a prison.

Faithful.
Uncompromising.
Unshaken.
He didn’t lose.
He fulfilled.
And Jesus Himself said, “Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).
Did you catch that?
Greatness in the Kingdom is not measured by how long you stay visible.
It’s measured by how faithfully you point to Jesus.
So let’s make this personal.
Where is your heart resisting decrease?
Where are you secretly competing with God for control?
Where are you building something that looks like ministry—but smells like self?
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Because the same Jesus John pointed to is the One who carried our pride to the cross.
The One who saw every moment we chose ourselves over Him—and still chose to die for us.
The One who rose again, not just to forgive you—but to free you.

Free you from the addiction to applause.
Free you from the fear of being forgotten.
Free you from the pressure to be everything.
You were never called to be the Savior.
You were called to know Him… and make Him known.
“He must increase.”

Not just in your words—but in your decisions.
Not just in your posts—but in your private life.
Not just in your ministry—but in your motives.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That is not a loss of identity.
That is the discovery of it.
So today—step down from the throne you were never meant to sit on.
Lay down the crown you were never meant to carry.
And let Jesus take His rightful place.
Because when He increases…

Grace increases.
Peace increases.
Purpose increases.
Life increases.
And you?
You don’t disappear.
You finally become whole.
Sit with it. Pray through it.

👉 It’s not about being seen.
👉 It’s about making Jesus seen.
